Arianism 4th century condemned Jesus is not fully God — a created being Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son of God was a created being — the first and greatest creature, exalted above all others, but not co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. His slogan became infamous: "There was a time when the Son was not." God could have no equal, Arius argued, and sharing His divine essence with another would compromise His absolute uniqueness. The Son was therefore a demigod — neither truly God nor truly man. "There was a time when the Son was not." — Arius Arius of Alexandria Eusebius of Nicomedia Emperor Constantius II Council of Nicaea (325 AD) — convened by Constantine, the Council declared that the Son is homoousios (of the same substance) as the Father. Arianism was formally condemned. Athanasius of Alexandria — "Athanasius contra mundum" (Athanasius against the world). Exiled five times for refusing to compromise, he alone seemed to hold the line. History vindicated him entirely. Council of Constantinople (381 AD) — reaffirmed Nicaea and extended the homoousios to the Holy Spirit, producing the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed still confessed in churches worldwide. The Nicene Creed — "God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father." Every word was chosen to exclude Arianism. Arianism never died — it only changed clothes. Jehovah's Witnesses teach classic Arianism: Jesus is a created being, "a god" but not the Almighty. Mormonism similarly denies the eternal co-equality of the Son. When a cult says "Jesus is not Jehovah," Athanasius has already answered them. The stakes are as high as ever: a Jesus who is merely the greatest creature cannot bear the infinite weight of our sin, and a Jesus who is not fully God cannot bring us to God. Nicene Creed (325/381); Athanasius, On the Incarnation (c. 318)

Docetism 1st–2nd century condemned Jesus only appeared to be human — the flesh is beneath God From the Greek dokein — "to seem" — Docetism taught that Christ did not truly take on human flesh but only appeared to do so. Influenced by Greek dualism's contempt for matter, Docetists could not accept that the divine Son would defile Himself with a real body. He walked on earth like a phantom: apparently hungry, apparently tired, apparently suffering — but not truly. The cross, on this view, was a divine illusion. "He suffered in appearance only, not in reality." — Docetist teaching as described by Ignatius Cerinthus Marcion (partially) Various Gnostic teachers Ignatius of Antioch (d. c. 108) — writing en route to his martyrdom, Ignatius hammered the physical reality of Christ's birth, suffering, and resurrection in every letter. "If, as some say, He suffered in appearance only... then why am I in bonds?" 1 John 4:2 — "By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God." John wrote this test of orthodoxy precisely to expose Docetism. Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) — defined Christ as truly God and truly man, with two complete natures, human and divine, united in one person without confusion or mixture. Docetism reappears wherever the physical reality of Christ's humanity is minimized. Some popular spirituality treats Jesus as a heavenly visitor who didn't really enter fully into human suffering, hunger, grief, and death. But the Gospel requires a fully human Savior — He had to be made like us "in every respect" (Heb. 2:17) to be our high priest. A phantom Christ cannot bear real sin, cannot truly die, and cannot truly rise. The resurrection is a bodily resurrection — or it is nothing. Ignatius of Antioch, Letters (c. 107–108); 1 John 4:1–3

Gnosticism 2nd–3rd century condemned Secret knowledge saves; the material world is evil; the Creator is not the true God Gnosticism was less a single movement than a family of heresies united by several convictions: that the material world is evil, created not by the supreme God but by a lower, ignorant or malevolent Demiurge (often identified with the God of the Old Testament); that a divine spark is imprisoned in human bodies; and that salvation comes through gnosis — secret spiritual knowledge available only to the enlightened. Christ, on this view, came to whisper the secret that releases souls from the prison of matter. The Creator of this world is an ignorant lesser power, not the true God. — the Gnostic view, as Irenaeus describes it Valentinus Basilides Marcion Carpocrates Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies (c. 180) — the most comprehensive refutation of Gnosticism ever written. Irenaeus systematically exposed every major Gnostic system and defended the unity of Scripture, the goodness of creation, and the physical resurrection. Tertullian — "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" He argued that Gnosticism was Greek philosophy smuggled into the church under Christian names. The Rule of Faith — the early church's summary of orthodox belief (ancestor of the Apostles' Creed) insisted on one God who is both Creator and Redeemer — directly countering Gnostic dualism. The biblical canon — Irenaeus's defense of the four Gospels (against Gnostic secret gospels) was a crucial step in the church's recognition of the New Testament canon. Gnosticism is the most durable heresy in Western culture. The Da Vinci Code, the Gospel of Judas media frenzy, and the entire New Age movement are Gnosticism in modern dress. The contempt for the body behind much sexual confusion ("I am a soul trapped in the wrong body"), the suspicion of the Old Testament God, and the cult of private spiritual experience over public doctrine — all are Gnostic instincts. Gnosticism's deepest appeal is pride: salvation by elite secret knowledge flatters the intellect and bypasses the humiliation of the cross. Irenaeus, Against Heresies (c. 180); Tertullian, Against Marcion (c. 208)

Health and Wealth Gospel 20th–21st century ongoing God guarantees physical health and financial prosperity to faithful believers The Prosperity Gospel — also called the Word of Faith movement or health-and-wealth gospel — teaches that God's will for every Christian is physical health and financial abundance, and that sickness or poverty are signs of weak faith or unconfessed sin. Faith is reframed as a spiritual force that, when exercised correctly (through positive confession and giving to the ministry), releases divine blessing. The atonement, on this view, purchased not just forgiveness but also healing and wealth. "God wants you well. God wants you rich. Name it and claim it." — common Word of Faith formula Kenneth Hagin Kenneth Copeland Joel Osteen Benny Hinn Creflo Dollar John MacArthur — has been perhaps the most consistent and courageous public critic of the Prosperity Gospel for decades. His books Charismatic Chaos and Strange Fire document the theological and pastoral devastation caused by these teachings. R.C. Sproul and other Reformed critics — identified the Prosperity Gospel as a fundamental distortion of the Gospel itself: it turns faith into a technique, God into a cosmic vending machine, and the cross into a transaction for earthly comfort rather than eternal redemption. John Piper — his Desiring God offers a sustained biblical alternative: God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in Him — not in His material gifts. The Bible itself — Job suffered righteously. Paul had a thorn he could not remove (2 Cor. 12). Christ was a man of sorrows. The apostles were beaten, imprisoned, and killed. The Prosperity Gospel cannot survive contact with the actual text of Scripture. The Prosperity Gospel is one of the fastest-growing forms of Christianity in the developing world, and it is leaving a trail of shattered faith in its wake. When the promised healing does not come — when the faithful believer dies of cancer, when the generous giver remains poor — the victim is told their faith was insufficient. The cruelty is staggering. The true Gospel offers something infinitely better than health and wealth: union with Christ, the forgiveness of sins, and an inheritance that moth and rust cannot destroy. John MacArthur, Charismatic Chaos (1992); Strange Fire (2013); D.A. Carson, How Long, O Lord? (1990)

Liberal Theology & Higher Criticism 18th century–present ongoing Scripture is a fallible human document — historically unreliable, culturally conditioned Arising from Enlightenment rationalism and developed through the 19th century German academy, liberal theology applied the historical-critical method to Scripture as it would to any ancient text — seeking to peel away layers of myth, legend, and editorial redaction to find a supposedly more primitive, authentic core. The supernatural was systematically removed: miracles became myths, the resurrection became a spiritual experience of the disciples, and Jesus became a moral teacher whose divine claims were later inventions of the church. "The Bible is the Word of God in the words of men — and the words of men err." — Liberal theological axiom Friedrich Schleiermacher Julius Wellhausen Adolf von Harnack Rudolf Bultmann John Shelby Spong The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) — signed by nearly 300 evangelical scholars including Sproul, Packer, and MacArthur, the Chicago Statement gave the church a precise, carefully worded affirmation of Scripture's complete truthfulness in all that it affirms. Article XII: "We deny that Biblical infallibility and inerrancy are limited to spiritual, religious, or redemptive themes." Every word was chosen to foreclose liberal evasions. R.C. Sproul — his Explaining Inerrancy and sustained defense of the Chicago Statement made him perhaps the foremost popular advocate for biblical inerrancy in the late 20th century. He argued that inerrancy is not a peripheral issue: if the Bible errs in any affirmation, the believer has no assured ground for trusting any of it. B.B. Warfield — his The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible (collected 1948) remains the most thorough scholarly defense of plenary verbal inspiration and inerrancy ever written. J. Gresham Machen — his Christianity and Liberalism (1923) made the decisive argument: liberal theology is not a revised Christianity but a different religion entirely. It retains Christian vocabulary while evacuating Christian content. Liberal theology has effectively destroyed mainline Protestantism. Every denomination that embraced it in the 20th century — Presbyterian Church USA, United Methodist Church, Episcopal Church — has seen decades of collapse, membership freefall, and the progressive abandonment of every distinctively Christian moral teaching. The pattern is familiar: first the Bible is no longer fully trusted, then the cross is reinterpreted, then the resurrection becomes metaphor, then sexual ethics are revised, then the Gospel itself evaporates. Machen saw it coming in 1923. The Chicago Statement was the line in the sand. Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978); J. Gresham Machen, Christianity and Liberalism (1923); B.B. Warfield, The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible (1948)

Modalism 2nd–3rd century condemned Father, Son, and Spirit are not three persons but one God wearing three masks Modalism (also called Sabellianism or Patripassianism) sought to protect monotheism by denying any real distinction between Father, Son, and Spirit. God is one person who appears in three successive modes or masks ( personae ): as Father in creation, as Son in the incarnation, and as Spirit in the church age. The attraction was obvious — this seemed to avoid both the charge of tritheism and the subordinationism of Arianism. But it destroyed the inner life of the Trinity and made the cross a monstrosity: who was the Father to whom Jesus prayed? "The Father himself was born, suffered, and died." — Patripassian formula Noetus of Smyrna Praxeas Sabellius Tertullian — coined the term trinitas and gave the church its essential formula: one substantia (substance), three personae (persons). His Against Praxeas is the first sustained Trinitarian theology. The Nicene Creed (325/381) — its careful language about the Son being "begotten of the Father before all worlds" and the Spirit "proceeding from the Father" preserves real personal distinctions within the one God. The Athanasian Creed — "We worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance." Its precision was developed directly to exclude both Arianism and Modalism. Modalism is the official theology of "Oneness Pentecostalism" (United Pentecostal Church), which baptizes only "in Jesus' name" and denies the Trinity. But softer modalism pervades evangelical worship: songs and sermons that treat Father, Son, and Spirit as interchangeable names for one undifferentiated God, or that speak of "the Father dying on the cross." The eternal, loving communion of three distinct persons is not a theological technicality — it is the heartbeat of the Gospel. The cross is the act of the eternal Son bearing the Father's just wrath, in the Spirit's power. Flatten the Trinity and the atonement collapses. Tertullian, Against Praxeas (c. 213); Athanasian Creed (c. 5th century)

Monophysitism 5th century condemned Christ has only one nature — the human was absorbed into the divine Eutyches of Constantinople, seeking to counter Nestorianism, swung to the opposite extreme: he taught that after the incarnation, Christ had only one nature — the human nature was absorbed into and overwhelmed by the divine, like a drop of vinegar in the sea. The result was neither truly God nor truly man but a tertium quid — a third thing. The name "Monophysitism" comes from the Greek: mono (one) + physis (nature). "I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union, one nature." — Eutyches Eutyches of Constantinople Dioscorus of Alexandria Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) — the most precise Christological statement in church history. Christ is "truly God and truly man... in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation." The four negative adverbs were surgical instruments designed to exclude both Nestorianism and Monophysitism simultaneously. Pope Leo I's Tome — read aloud at Chalcedon, it prompted the bishops to cry: "Peter has spoken through Leo!" It articulated how the two natures operate: each nature acts in communion with the other according to its own properties. Chalcedon's "two natures" formula is not ecclesiastical hair-splitting — it is the grammar of salvation. A Christ with only one nature cannot be our mediator. The mediator between God and man must be both God and man — fully, not partially. He must be fully man to represent us, fully God to save us. The Coptic and Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which call their view Miaphysite and reject Eutyches, still stand outside Chalcedon, producing ongoing ecumenical dialogue about this fifth-century fault line. Definition of Chalcedon (451); Leo I, Tome (449)

Moralistic Therapeutic Deism 21st century ongoing God wants you to be nice, feel good, and stay out of the way Named and diagnosed by sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton in their 2005 study of American teenage religion, Moralistic Therapeutic Deism (MTD) is not a formal movement but the actual functional religion of millions of churchgoing Americans. Its five tenets: (1) A God exists who created the world and set up a moral order. (2) God wants people to be nice and fair to each other. (3) The central goal of life is to be happy and feel good about yourself. (4) God does not need to be involved in your life unless you have a problem. (5) Good people go to heaven when they die. No sin, no cross, no resurrection, no repentance, no discipleship. "God is something like a combination Divine Butler and Cosmic Therapist." — Christian Smith & Melinda Lundquist Denton No formal founders — the ambient theology of therapeutic culture absorbed into the church R.C. Sproul — his entire ministry was an assault on MTD before the term existed. The holiness of God, the bondage of the will, the necessity of justification by faith alone — all are direct antidotes to MTD's self-satisfied moralism. John MacArthur, The Gospel According to Jesus (1988) — challenged the "easy believism" that produces MTD-style converts: people who have prayed a prayer but show no marks of regeneration, no love of Scripture, no cross-bearing discipleship. Paul Washer — his confrontational 2002 "Shocking Youth Message" went viral precisely because it named the MTD reality most youth ministries had been producing and called it what it is: a false conversion. The Reformation catechisms — Westminster Shorter Catechism Q1: "What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." Not to be happy. Not to feel good. To glorify God. The catechism is the curriculum MTD forgot. MTD is the water most Western churchgoers swim in. It explains why self-identified Christians in surveys hold views indistinguishable from their secular neighbors on every moral question, why church attendance has collapsed even among those who claim to believe, and why preaching that costs nothing produces converts who are worth nothing. The antidote is not harsher religion but the actual Gospel: a holy God, a real sin, an atoning cross, an empty tomb, a risen Lord, a coming judgment, and a grace so great it transforms everything it touches. Christian Smith & Melinda Denton, Soul Searching (2005); Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647)

Nestorianism 5th century condemned Christ is two separate persons — divine and human — loosely joined Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos ("God-bearer" or "Mother of God"), preferring Christotokos ("Christ-bearer"). Behind this terminological dispute lay a deeper theological problem: Nestorius seemed to teach that the divine and human in Christ were so distinct as to constitute two separate persons — a divine Christ and a human Jesus joined in a kind of moral or sympathetic union. The unity of Christ's person was dissolved. "I cannot call a two- or three-month-old infant God." — Nestorius, objecting to Theotokos Nestorius of Constantinople Theodore of Mopsuestia Cyril of Alexandria — insisted on the communicatio idiomatum (communication of attributes): what is true of either nature can be attributed to the one person of Christ. Therefore Mary truly bore God incarnate — the eternal Son took her flesh. Council of Ephesus (431 AD) — condemned Nestorianism and affirmed Theotokos. Nestorius was deposed and exiled. The Nestorian church survived in Persia and spread as far as China, where the 8th-century Xi'an Stele records missionaries arriving in 635. Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) — gave the definitive formula: one person (hypostasis), two natures. The person is undivided even as the natures are unmixed. Nestorianism's practical consequence is a Christ who cannot save: if the divine and human are merely morally united in one body, then the suffering on the cross belongs to the human Jesus alone and cannot carry infinite weight. The infinite dignity of the atonement requires that it is the eternal Son of God who suffers — not a human being with whom the Son happens to be associated. One person suffered. One person rose. One person sits at the Father's right hand interceding for us. Cyril of Alexandria, On the Unity of Christ (c. 437); Definition of Chalcedon (451)

Open Theism Late 20th century–present ongoing God does not know the future — He learns and adjusts as history unfolds Open Theism, developed within evangelical Christianity in the 1990s, teaches that God does not have exhaustive foreknowledge of future free human choices. To preserve genuine human freedom, God limits His knowledge of the future — the future is "open" even to Him. He makes His best plans, takes risks, and responds in real time to the choices of His creatures. Proponents argued this makes God more relational and prayer more meaningful. The future is partly settled and partly open, even to God. — Gregory Boyd's position (God of the Possible, 2000), summarised Clark Pinnock Gregory Boyd John Sanders Richard Rice R.C. Sproul — argued that a God who does not know the future is not the God of Scripture. The God of Scripture declares "the end from the beginning" (Isa. 46:10). A God who takes risks is a God who might lose. John Piper — his Beyond the Bounds (edited with Justin Taylor) gathered Reformed scholars to respond comprehensively to Open Theism's biblical and philosophical claims. John Frame, No Other God (2001) — the most thorough philosophical and biblical refutation of Open Theism, showing that the God of Scripture is immutable, omniscient, and sovereign over all events including free human choices. Evangelical Theological Society (2001) — passed a resolution affirming that God has complete and infallible knowledge of all future events, including human decisions; a 2003 attempt to expel two leading open theists fell short. Open Theism seems to make God more relatable — a companion on a shared journey into an unknown future. But the comfort it offers is fraudulent. A God who does not know whether the cancer will be cured, whether the prodigal will return, whether history will reach its appointed end, cannot give genuine assurance to a dying saint. The God of Scripture does not take risks. He ordains the end from the beginning, and nothing — not the fall of a sparrow, not the fall of a kingdom — falls outside His sovereign knowledge and will. That God alone is worth trusting. John Frame, No Other God (2001); John Piper & Justin Taylor, eds., Beyond the Bounds (2003)

Pelagianism 5th century condemned Man can achieve salvation by his own free will — grace is helpful but not necessary Pelagius, a British monk who arrived in Rome around 380 AD, was scandalized by what he saw as moral laxity among Christians who blamed their sin on human weakness. He taught that Adam's sin affected only Adam — not the human race. Human nature is not fallen or corrupted; every person is born with the same capacity for righteousness that Adam possessed. Grace is helpful — God's teaching, example, and forgiveness — but it is not the necessary cause of any good deed. A person can, in principle, achieve holiness by free moral effort. "If I ought, I can." — The Pelagian principle Pelagius Caelestius Julian of Eclanum Augustine of Hippo — the greatest theological battle of his career was against Pelagianism. Augustine's doctrines of original sin, total depravity, irresistible grace, and sovereign election were hammered out on the anvil of the Pelagian controversy. Council of Carthage (418 AD) — condemned Pelagianism in a series of canons, affirming original sin, the inheritance of spiritual death from Adam, and the necessity of God's grace for every good work. Council of Orange (529 AD) — further refined the church's anti-Pelagian consensus, affirming that even the will to believe is a gift of God's grace. Pelagianism is the natural religion of the human heart. Every instinct of fallen humanity wants to contribute something to salvation — to be the hero of its own redemption story. It reappears in every era: the medieval doctrine of merit, Arminian synergism, modern self-help Christianity, the prosperity gospel's "your faith releases God's blessing." The Reformation's sola gratia is a direct, thundering refusal of Pelagian logic. Salvation is of the Lord — entirely, root and branch, from first to last. Augustine, On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin (418); Canons of the Council of Orange (529)

Roman Catholic System 16th century controversy (system developed medievally) ongoing Works, tradition, and sacraments co-operate with grace for salvation; the Pope speaks infallibly The Reformers' quarrel with Rome was not over peripheral matters but over the Gospel itself. The Roman system, as defined at the Council of Trent (1545–1563), taught that justification is not the imputation of Christ's righteousness but an interior transformation that makes the sinner progressively righteous; that this righteousness can be augmented by meritorious works; that those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified must pass through purgatory; that the Mass is a propitiatory sacrifice re-presenting Christ's offering; and that the Pope, when speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals, is infallible. Scripture and Church Tradition are co-equal sources of authority. "If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified... let him be anathema." — Council of Trent, Session VI, Canon 9 Council of Trent (1545–1563) Vatican I (1870, papal infallibility) Vatican II (1962–65) Martin Luther — his Ninety-Five Theses (1517) attacked indulgences as a symptom of a system that had commercialized grace. His deeper discovery — that justification is by faith alone, through Christ's imputed righteousness — was the theological earthquake of the millennium. John Calvin — his Institutes gave the Reformed world its systematic alternative to Rome on every contested point: Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, glory to God alone. Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) — Chapter XI defines justification with precision forged in controversy: God imputes Christ's obedience and satisfaction to the sinner, received by faith alone, not from anything wrought in or done by them. R.C. Sproul — his book Faith Alone and his response to the "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" document (1994) kept the Reformation's central issue on the evangelical agenda when many were ready to set it aside. The Reformation is not over. The Council of Trent's anathemas on justification by faith alone have never been lifted. Rome's official theology still teaches that the righteousness by which we stand before God is partly our own transformed character — not solely the alien righteousness of Christ imputed. For Sproul, this was not a secondary disagreement between brothers but a question of whether sinners are told the truth about how to be right with God. The five Solas are not museum pieces; they are life and death. Luther, Freedom of a Christian (1520); Westminster Confession Ch. XI; Sproul, Faith Alone (1995)

Semi-Pelagianism 5th century–present condemned Man takes the first step toward God; grace assists the rest Semi-Pelagianism was a mediating position developed by monks in southern Gaul who found Augustine's sovereignty of grace too severe. They accepted original sin and the need for grace but insisted that the human will takes the first step — the initial movement toward faith — and God then cooperates with and strengthens that decision. Salvation begins with man's unaided desire for God; grace follows and completes it. This preserved human initiative and softened the sharp edges of Augustinian predestination. "The beginning of faith and the good will are from ourselves; the completion is from God." — Semi-Pelagian position as condemned at Orange John Cassian Faustus of Riez Vincent of Lérins Council of Orange (529 AD) — condemned Semi-Pelagianism explicitly, declaring that even the first inclination toward faith is the gift of God's grace, not a human achievement. Augustine — met the first stirrings of the debate in his last works, insisting that even the will to seek God is a divine gift. "Our heart is restless until it rests in Thee" — and even that restlessness is grace-given. The Reformation's doctrine of Total Depravity — the "T" in TULIP is the Reformed answer to Semi-Pelagianism. The unregenerate will is in bondage; it does not and cannot take a first step toward God apart from prevenient and effectual grace. Semi-Pelagianism is the default theology of most contemporary evangelicalism, even where it is not consciously held. Every altar call that says "God has done His part — now it's up to you" is Semi-Pelagian. Every theology that makes election dependent on God's foresight of human faith comes close to it. It is more comfortable than Calvinism, more orthodox than Pelagianism, and more wrong than either: it gives man the first and decisive word in his own salvation, which is precisely the ground the Reformation refused to concede. Canons of Orange (529); Augustine, On the Predestination of the Saints (429)

Socinianism 16th–17th century condemned Denial of the Trinity, the pre-existence of Christ, and penal substitution Developed by Fausto Sozzini (Socinus) in 16th-century Poland, Socinianism was a radical rationalist theology that rejected every doctrine it found philosophically incoherent: the Trinity (one God in three persons is logically contradictory), the pre-existence of Christ (He was a uniquely inspired human teacher, not the eternal Son), and penal substitutionary atonement (it is unjust for an innocent party to bear another's guilt). Salvation is moral influence and example — Christ shows us how to live, not how to be forgiven. The Trinity is neither taught in Scripture nor consistent with reason. — the Racovian Catechism (1605), summarised Lelio Sozzini Fausto Sozzini (Socinus) The Polish Brethren Racovian Catechism John Owen, A Dissertation on Divine Justice (1653) — the most thorough Reformed response to the Socinian rejection of penal substitution, demonstrating from Scripture and natural theology that God's justice necessarily demands satisfaction for sin. Francis Turretin — his Institutes of Elenctic Theology engaged every Socinian argument systematically, producing what many regard as the finest scholastic Reformed theology ever written. Reformed confessions broadly — the Westminster Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Belgic Confession all affirm the Trinity, the eternal Sonship, and penal substitution in direct opposition to Socinian denials. Socinianism is the ancestor of modern Unitarianism, theological liberalism's rejection of substitutionary atonement, and much of contemporary "progressive Christianity." When a pastor says "I don't believe in a God who requires a blood sacrifice" or "Jesus died as a moral example, not to absorb divine wrath," they are teaching Socinianism — usually without knowing its name. The answer is John Owen: the God who is perfectly just cannot simply overlook sin. The cross is not primitive barbarity but the only place in the universe where justice and mercy truly kiss. John Owen, A Dissertation on Divine Justice (1653); Heidelberg Catechism Q. 40 (1563)

Adoptionism 2nd–8th century condemned Jesus was a mere man whom God "adopted" as His Son at His baptism or resurrection Adoptionism taught that Jesus was born an ordinary human being and was elevated — adopted — to divine Sonship either at His baptism (when the Spirit descended), at His resurrection, or at His ascension. There was no eternal pre-existence of the Son; Jesus became divine by moral achievement and divine appointment. Two main forms appeared: the early Dynamic Monarchianism of Paul of Samosata, and the later Spanish Adoptionism of Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgel in the 8th century. Jesus was a mere man who by moral progress and divine grace was adopted into Sonship. — Paul of Samosata's teaching, summarised Paul of Samosata Theodotus of Byzantium Elipandus of Toledo Felix of Urgel Council of Antioch (268 AD) — condemned Paul of Samosata and deposed him as Bishop of Antioch. The council rejected his teaching that the Logos was not a distinct person but merely an attribute of God operating in the man Jesus. The Nicene Creed (325 AD) — its affirmation that the Son is "begotten of the Father before all worlds" and "God of God, Light of Light" directly excluded any form of adoptionism. Council of Frankfurt (794 AD) — convened by Charlemagne, condemned the Spanish Adoptionism of Elipandus and Felix. Adoptionism is the functional Christology of much liberal Christianity and countless Christmas sermons that present Jesus as the supreme human example who "shows us what God is like." The moment Jesus becomes merely a uniquely God-filled man rather than the eternal Son become flesh, the atonement collapses. An adopted son cannot bear the infinite weight of infinite sin. Only one who is truly and eternally God can save — not because He earned it, but because He is it. Nicene Creed (325); Council of Frankfurt canons (794)

Antinomianism 16th century–present ongoing The law of God has no place in the Christian life — grace abolishes obligation Antinomianism (from Greek: anti + nomos , "against law") teaches that because Christians are under grace and not law, the moral law of God has no binding authority over them. In its most radical form, no sin committed by a believer can affect their standing before God, and preaching the law is a denial of grace. Luther's disciple Johannes Agricola triggered the first major controversy; it has reappeared in every generation, most recently in hyper-grace teaching. "Away with Moses to the gallows!" — the antinomian slogan, as Luther reported it Johannes Agricola John Eaton (17th c.) Tobias Crisp (17th c.) Joseph Prince (contemporary) Martin Luther — wrote a series of disputations against antinomianism, insisting that the law must still be preached to convict sinners. Melanchthon and Calvin later spoke of three uses of the law: civil restraint, conviction of sin, and guidance for the regenerate ( tertius usus legis ) — the third especially important to the Reformed tradition. John Calvin — his doctrine of the third use of the law (the law as guide for the redeemed) is the classic Reformed answer. The law does not save; but once saved, believers delight in it as the revealed will of the God they love (Ps. 119:97). The Westminster Confession, Chapter XIX — "The moral law doth for ever bind all, as well justified persons as others, to the obedience thereof... Neither doth Christ in the Gospel any way dissolve, but much strengthen this obligation." Walter Marshall, John Owen, Samuel Bolton — Puritan theologians produced the most careful accounts of law and grace, showing that the law drives to Christ and Christ sends back to the law — not for justification but for sanctification. Antinomianism is the permanent temptation of grace-centered preaching. Every generation that recovers the free grace of justification faces the charge Paul anticipated: "Shall we sin that grace may abound?" (Rom. 6:1). The Reformed answer is never "you must obey to stay saved" — that is legalism. It is always "you are dead to sin and alive to God — therefore do not let sin reign" (Rom. 6:11–12). Genuine grace produces holy living; it does not excuse ungodly living. The tree is known by its fruit. Westminster Confession Ch. XIX; Calvin, Institutes III.vi–x; Samuel Bolton, The True Bounds of Christian Freedom (1645)

Apollinarianism 4th century condemned Christ had no human mind — the divine Logos replaced His rational soul Apollinaris of Laodicea, a close ally of Athanasius and a fierce opponent of Arianism, attempted to explain the unity of Christ's person by teaching that the divine Logos took the place of the rational human soul ( nous ) in Jesus. Christ had a human body and a human spirit, but not a human mind — the Logos supplied the intellectual and volitional faculty. This preserved His sinlessness (a human mind would sin) but destroyed His full humanity. Christ's flesh came from heaven, and the Word took the place of a human mind. — the teaching his opponents charged him with Apollinaris of Laodicea Gregory of Nazianzus — delivered the decisive theological refutation: "What has not been assumed has not been healed." If Christ did not take on a human mind, then human minds are unredeemed. The Incarnation must be complete or the salvation it effects is incomplete. Council of Constantinople (381 AD) — condemned Apollinarianism along with Arianism and affirmed that Christ took on full and complete human nature — body, soul, and mind. Gregory's axiom — "what has not been assumed has not been healed" — is one of the most important sentences in the history of theology. It means that the extent of our salvation depends on the extent of the Incarnation. Christ had to be fully human — including a human will that struggled, a human mind that grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), a human soul that was troubled (John 12:27) — so that every dimension of our fallen humanity could be redeemed. A partial Savior saves partially. The church's insistence on full humanity is not philosophical pedantry; it is pastoral comfort. Gregory of Nazianzus, Epistle 101 (c. 382); Canons of Constantinople (381)

Donatism 4th–5th century condemned The church must be visibly pure — sacraments from sinful ministers are invalid The Donatist controversy arose in North Africa when a group of bishops refused to accept the ordination of Caecilian of Carthage because one of his consecrators had reportedly handed over Scriptures to Roman authorities during persecution (the traditores — "handers-over," root of the word "traitor"). The Donatists insisted that the church must be a community of the visibly holy, and that sacraments administered by sinful or apostate clergy are null and void. The validity of the sacrament, they taught, depends on the moral purity of the minister. "What has the Emperor to do with the Church?" — Donatus of Carthage Donatus of Carthage Parmenian Petilian of Constantine Augustine of Hippo — devoted enormous energy to refuting Donatism. His key distinction: the validity of the sacrament depends on Christ, not the minister. The sacrament is Christ's, not the priest's; a wicked minister baptizes with Christ's baptism, not his own. The ex opere operato principle — though later misused by Rome, the kernel was Augustine's: the efficacy of the sacrament does not depend on the worthiness of the administrator but on the promise of Christ attached to it. Council of Arles (314 AD) and subsequent imperial legislation — repeatedly condemned Donatism; re-baptisms by Donatists were declared invalid. Donatism reappears wherever Christians demand visible purity as the condition of valid ministry or genuine church membership. The impulse is understandable — holiness matters. But the Reformed tradition, following Augustine, insists that the church in this age is a corpus permixtum — a mixed body of wheat and tares (Matt. 13:24–30). The marks of a true church are the pure preaching of the Word and the right administration of the sacraments — not the verified holiness of its ministers. Every pastoral failure that triggers a church split over purity is Donatism in a new dress. Augustine, On Baptism Against the Donatists (c. 400); Letters 93, 185

Hyper-Calvinism 18th century–present ongoing God's sovereign election means we should not indiscriminately offer the Gospel to all Hyper-Calvinism is not Calvinism taken to its logical conclusion — it is Calvinism distorted by a failure to distinguish between God's secret will and His revealed will. It typically includes one or more of: denying that there is a genuine, well-meant offer of the Gospel to all sinners; denying that unregenerate people have any duty to repent and believe; teaching that only the elect should be urged to come to Christ; or refusing to pray for the salvation of all people. It arose most prominently in 18th-century English Particular Baptist circles. "We should not offer Christ to sinners indiscriminately — only the elect are warranted to believe." — Hyper-Calvinist position John Gill (in tendencies) Joseph Hussey John Brine Andrew Fuller, The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785) — the decisive Reformed refutation of hyper-Calvinism. Fuller argued that all sinners are obligated to believe the Gospel, and that the free offer of the Gospel is fully consistent with particular election. His theology enabled William Carey's missionary movement. Charles Spurgeon — preached sovereign grace with passionate evangelistic urgency, in a saying often attributed to him: "If God had painted a yellow stripe down the back of every elect person, I would go up and down the streets lifting up coat-tails. But since He hasn't, I preach the Gospel to every person I meet." John Murray & Ned Stonehouse, "The Free Offer of the Gospel" (1948) — the classic 20th-century Reformed paper demonstrating from Scripture that God genuinely desires the salvation of all, even while sovereignly electing some — the distinction between His decretive and preceptive will. Hyper-Calvinism is the death of evangelism. If the Gospel is only for the elect, and the elect are unknown to us, the missionary impulse is paralyzed. Historically, hyper-Calvinism produced exactly this: churches that grew cold, inward, and fruitless. The recovery of the free offer — "whosoever will may come" — by Fuller, Spurgeon, and the Princeton theologians unleashed the modern missionary movement. Sovereign grace and passionate evangelism are not opposites; they are the engine and the fuel of genuine Reformed mission. Andrew Fuller, The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785); Murray & Stonehouse, The Free Offer of the Gospel (1948)

Marcionism 2nd century condemned The God of the Old Testament is a different, inferior God — the New Testament alone is Scripture Marcion of Sinope arrived in Rome around 140 AD with a radical thesis: the wrathful, law-giving God of the Old Testament is not the Father of Jesus Christ. The OT God is the Demiurge — a just but inferior deity who created the material world and made demands of his creatures. Jesus revealed a higher, previously unknown God of pure love and mercy. Marcion produced the first canon of Scripture: an edited Gospel of Luke (with all OT references removed) and ten letters of Paul (similarly edited). Everything Jewish was excised. The God of the Law is not the Father of Jesus Christ. — Marcion's teaching, as Tertullian reports it Marcion of Sinope Marcionite churches (spread across the Empire for centuries) Tertullian, Against Marcion (5 books, c. 208 AD) — the most thorough patristic refutation of any heresy. Tertullian demonstrated from Scripture and reason that the God of the OT and NT is one God, that the OT is fulfilled — not abolished — in Christ, and that Marcion's edited Bible is an act of mutilation. Irenaeus, Against Heresies — showed that Marcion destroyed the entire economy of salvation: no creation, no fall, no law, no prophecy, no real incarnation — and therefore no real redemption. The biblical canon — the church's rejection of Marcion's truncated Bible and its eventual affirmation of the full OT-NT canon was a direct response to the Marcionite challenge. The canon is, in part, an anti-Marcionite document. Marcionism is the most persistently recurring heresy in church history. Every generation produces Christians who are embarrassed by the OT — its warfare, its judgment, its demands — and want a Jesus of pure love untainted by Sinai. Liberal Christianity's selective use of Scripture, the dismissal of OT ethics as "sub-Christian," and the sentimental reduction of God to pure affirmation — all are Marcionite instincts. The answer is what it always was: the God who spoke at Sinai is the Father of Jesus Christ. The wrath and the mercy are one God's. The cross is where they meet. Tertullian, Against Marcion (c. 208); Irenaeus, Against Heresies Bk. III (c. 180)

Montanism 2nd–3rd century condemned New prophecy supersedes Scripture — the Spirit speaks fresh revelation through living prophets Around 165 AD in Phrygia, a convert named Montanus began speaking in ecstatic trances, claiming to be the mouthpiece of the Holy Spirit. Two prophetesses, Prisca and Maximilla, joined him. They proclaimed a new outpouring of the Spirit that completed and superseded Scripture, announced the imminent end of the world, and demanded extreme asceticism — fasting, celibacy, willingness for martyrdom. Maximilla announced: "After me there will be no more prophetess, but the end." The world did not end. Tertullian, the great defender of orthodoxy, eventually joined them. "I am the Father, the Word, and the Paraclete." — words later ascribed to Montanus, speaking as the Spirit Montanus of Phrygia Prisca Maximilla Tertullian (later) Synods in Asia Minor (c. 177 AD) — local church councils condemned Montanism and excommunicated its adherents, the first recorded use of synodical condemnation of heresy. Anonymous anti-Montanist writer (cited by Eusebius) — challenged Montanus's prophecies on the grounds that genuine prophecy does not come in ecstatic trance, which removes rational control, but in the prophet's conscious awareness. The principle of the closed canon — the church's growing recognition of a defined New Testament canon was sharpened precisely by the Montanist crisis. If the Spirit could add to Scripture through living prophets, Scripture could never be the final authority. Montanism is the ancient template for every movement that claims fresh revelation superseding or supplementing Scripture. The New Apostolic Reformation's claim to living apostles and prophets with binding authority, certain charismatic movements' "words from the Lord" that contradict or go beyond the Bible, and the Mormon claim to an ongoing prophet — all follow the Montanist pattern. The Reformed answer: the canon is closed. The Spirit does not whisper new doctrines to selected vessels; He illumines the sufficient Word already given. Sola Scriptura was forged partly in the fire of Montanism. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History V.16–19; B.B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles (1918)

New Apostolic Reformation Late 20th century–present ongoing God has restored living apostles and prophets with binding authority to establish His kingdom on earth The New Apostolic Reformation (NAR), a term coined by missiologist C. Peter Wagner, teaches that God is restoring the five-fold ministry of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers (Eph. 4:11) — particularly apostles and prophets — with authority comparable to the biblical originals. These living apostles and prophets receive direct revelation from God, issue binding spiritual directives, engage in territorial spiritual warfare, and are building a global network to bring about the Kingdom of God before Christ returns (a form of dominionism). God has restored the offices of apostle and prophet to govern the church today. — C. Peter Wagner's teaching, summarised C. Peter Wagner Bill Johnson (Bethel Church) Cindy Jacobs Rick Joyner Mike Bickle (IHOP) John MacArthur, Strange Fire (2013) — the most comprehensive recent evangelical critique of the charismatic and NAR movements, documenting their departure from Scripture and the fruit of false prophecy, manipulative practice, and doctrinal confusion. The cessationist argument — the foundational and revelatory gifts (apostles, prophets in the canonical sense) ceased with the closing of the canon (Eph. 2:20: the church is built on the foundation of apostles and prophets — foundations are laid once). Living "apostles" claiming canonical authority are claiming what Scripture does not permit. The test of the prophet (Deut. 18:20–22) — a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken from God and shall be put to death. Documented failures of NAR prophetic predictions — including prophecies about the 2020 US election widely circulated and later retracted — are not merely embarrassments but, by the biblical standard, disqualifications. The NAR is one of the fastest-growing streams of global Christianity and one of the most dangerous movements in the contemporary church from a Reformed perspective. It combines the Montanist error (new revelation), the prosperity gospel's triumphalism, and a dominionist political theology — all under the banner of the Holy Spirit. MacArthur's warning stands: the Spirit's name is taken in vain whenever human authority, spiritual manipulation, or unverified "prophecy" is wrapped in His person. The Spirit does not contradict the Word He inspired. John MacArthur, Strange Fire (2013); D.A. Carson, Showing the Spirit (1987); Deut. 18:20–22

Universalism 19th century–present ongoing All people will ultimately be saved — God's love cannot permit eternal condemnation Universalism teaches that all human beings will ultimately be reconciled to God — that hell, if it exists, is remedial and temporary, and that God's love will finally triumph over every human rejection. It ranges from the soft universalism of "hopeful universalism" (we may hope all are saved) to the confident universalism of Thomas Talbott and Rob Bell's popular Love Wins — with Karl Barth's doctrine of election pointing that way, though he refused the label. The driving conviction: an all-loving, all-powerful God cannot be eternally defeated by human sin. "Does God get what God wants?" — chapter title, Rob Bell, Love Wins (2011) Origen (apokatastasis) Friedrich Schleiermacher Karl Barth (ambiguously) Rob Bell Thomas Talbott The words of Jesus Himself — more warnings about hell fall from the lips of Jesus than from any other figure in Scripture. "These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matt. 25:46). The same word ( aionios ) modifies both destinies. You cannot have eternal life without eternal punishment. R.C. Sproul — insisted that universalism makes the cross unnecessary. If all are saved, why did Christ die? The substitutionary atonement requires that someone bears God's wrath — and those outside Christ bear it themselves, eternally. D.A. Carson, The Gagging of God (1996) — the most thorough evangelical response to pluralism and universalism, showing that Scripture consistently and clearly teaches eternal, conscious punishment for those who die outside Christ. Francis Chan & Preston Sprinkle, Erasing Hell (2011) — written directly in response to Rob Bell, surveying every NT passage on eternal punishment and concluding that hell is real, conscious, and eternal. Universalism is ultimately an act of editorial revision: taking the parts of Scripture about God's love and deleting the parts about God's wrath and final judgment. But the same Bible that says "God is love" (1 John 4:8) says "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Heb. 10:31). The doctrine of hell is not a peripheral theological curiosity — it is the dark backdrop that makes the Gospel news. Without the wrath from which we flee, there is no grace to which we run. The urgency of every faithful sermon depends on it. D.A. Carson, The Gagging of God (1996); Francis Chan & Preston Sprinkle, Erasing Hell (2011); Matt. 25:46
